stories.headline: Update: Trump Excoriates Zelensky, Says He 'Probably Never' Wanted to End War, After Ukraine's Drone Strikes on Russia
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did." The remarks followed one of Ukraine's largest drone attacks of the year on Russia, which hit a key oil terminal in defiance of Trump's demand that Kyiv stop striking Russian energy infrastructure. Trump wrote that he is negotiating peace and does not want to "foolishly" drive Russia away from the bargaining table, adding that he believes "great progress is being made."

Russia's defense ministry said it shot down 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight. Among the targets was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, which can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year; Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said a fire broke out on its grounds. A logistics center and a data center for the VKontakte social network were also reportedly hit. Local authorities said one person was killed and five wounded, with residential homes damaged.

The exchange follows Trump's Friday decision to invoke a waiver exempting Russia from sanctions mandated by Congress, a move that drew bipartisan criticism. Zelensky told NBC's "Meet the Press" that the United States siding with Russia would be a "historic mistake." Last week Trump called Ukraine's refinery strikes a "disgrace" and said both sides had agreed to stop attacking energy infrastructure, though neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such a deal. The White House is seeking to ease oil and diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections.

Despite the public rupture, Zelensky said he spoke Sunday with US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of "nonstop communication," and wrote that Ukraine is doing everything to ensure "America's position is strong and helps bring peace closer." Kyiv fears losing essential US support heading into another winter of Russian attacks.

stories.headline: Midterm Fight: Conway and Lake Warn Poll Leads May Not Translate to Turnout
stories.summary:
On Sunday political shows, strategists from both parties cautioned that polling advantages ahead of the midterm elections may not decide the outcome. Republican commentator Kellyanne Conway said on "Fox News Sunday" that "participation in a poll is not the same as participation at the polls." She argued that some Republicans are reluctant to answer surveys and that competitive Senate races remain "on a razor's edge."

Conway also questioned election prediction markets, saying they cannot reliably determine who will actually vote. Her comments came as Democrats hold leads in several polls and in fundraising, including a recent survey showing President Trump's approval at a record low.

Democratic pollster Celinda Lake, a former Biden campaign pollster, agreed that Democrats lead on enthusiasm but urged voters not to let favorable polls keep them home. "It's important for people at this point in time not to listen to the polls," she said. Lake also acknowledged her party has made insufficient investment in youth turnout, crediting Republicans and Turning Point USA with doing a better job on that front.

Control of the Senate hangs on a handful of close contests, and early voting is under way in many states. Both parties are now focused on converting enthusiasm and polling into actual ballots in the final weeks of the campaign.

stories.headline: Update: Historic Limoges Town Hall Set Ablaze After Nationwide French Protests
stories.summary:
The 19th-century town hall in the French city of Limoges was damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests on Saturday. Footage shared online showed the building engulfed in flames, and the spire of its clock tower later collapsed. Firefighters battled the blaze through the night.

On Sunday, stunned residents watched as crews assessed the structure's integrity. Officials have not confirmed whether the building is at risk of collapse. One resident told the BBC that damaging heritage buildings because of anger at the government is "selfish."

The fire adds to widespread damage from the unrest across France, where about 1,800 people have been arrested. Authorities are expected to investigate the arson and determine the extent of the structural damage in the coming days.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Approval Falls to Record Low of 33 Percent, Giving Democrats Midterm Edge
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump's job approval has fallen to 33 percent, the lowest of his presidency, with 66 percent disapproving and just over half saying they disapprove strongly, according to a poll reported by The Washington Post. The survey also shows rising support for Democrats in the generic midterm ballot, roughly two weeks before the November 3 elections.

The findings come as Democrats have posted record fundraising totals and as the electoral battlefield has widened into states that usually favor Republicans, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. Analysts on Bloomberg said Trump's weak ratings give Democrats several paths to Senate control. Democrats are also counting on Latino-heavy House districts in Arizona, Colorado and Texas, where they hope disaffected Trump voters will swing back.

The White House has faced turmoil in recent days, including the ouster of press secretary Katie Zacharia after five days and reports that chief of staff Susie Wiles may have lost the president's confidence. Former chief of staff Mick Mulvaney said he expects Wiles to leave after the midterms on her own terms. Some Republican candidates are avoiding mention of Trump in their ads, and a number have declined to appear with him at events.

Trump and his allies have argued that Republicans can hold their ground by emphasizing immigration enforcement and the administration's handling of the Iran war. Democrats say voters are reacting to high costs, including gas prices that have risen during the conflict. Polls are snapshots, and turnout will determine how far the shift translates into seats.

stories.headline: Update: Top Aides Give Conflicting Defenses of Russia Diesel Deal as Republicans Join Criticism
stories.summary:
Trump administration officials offered sharply different explanations on Sunday talk shows for the president's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy, while also striking a diesel export deal with Moscow. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the waivers did not amount to sanctions relief, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright defended the move on ABC's "This Week." Wright also faced questions on CNN about earlier predictions that gas prices would fall quickly, as the Iran war enters its eighth month.

Criticism came from both parties. Sen. Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, said on CBS that "capitulating to a bully generally means they're going to make more demands going forward." Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio called for a congressional investigation into Starlink disruptions in Ukraine, and former Vice President Mike Pence urged Trump to restore the sanctions. Democrats have called the move a gift to Putin, and a bipartisan effort to overturn the diesel deal is expected when Congress returns after the election.

Trump said he acted so as not to drive Putin away from peace talks and to ease fuel prices in the United States. He also criticized Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries and said he finds Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky harder to deal with than Putin. Zelensky told NBC's "Meet the Press" that Ukraine trusts America and hopes Trump will "change his decisions," and that backing Putin would be a "historic mistake."

Zelensky later said he held a roughly 40-minute call with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the first senior contact since tensions spiked, and that new rounds of peace talks could be arranged as early as this week. The UK government has signaled it disagrees with Washington's approach.

stories.headline: Update: Alberta Prepares for Monday Vote on Starting Legal Path Toward Separation Referendum
stories.summary:
Voters in Alberta, Canada's oil-producing province, will decide on Monday, October 19, whether to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on leaving Canada. The vote does not itself trigger separation. Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote but supports staying in Canada, said support for starting the process, around 23 percent in a recent poll, is "still too high for my liking."

Alberta holds the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves and has long feuded with Ottawa over energy and federal power, particularly under Liberal governments that imposed a carbon tax and other climate measures. Separatist parties historically drew only 1 to 2 percent of the vote, according to former Premier Jason Kenney. He told the Associated Press the movement grew from the 2022 Freedom Convoy and pandemic-era anger, and became more professional as it built organizations and raised money.

Independence leaders such as Jeff Rath say vaccine rules were their breaking point. Kenney also sees overlap between some activists and supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin or conspiracy theories, a characterization separatists may dispute.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has campaigned for national unity, including at a Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton, and has said the United States is trying to break Canada. The result will indicate how much appetite exists for separation and could shape Canada's politics and its relationship with Washington. This comes as Canada is also mourning four service members killed in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Endorses Netanyahu Ahead of Oct. 27 Israeli Election, Warns Exit Could Deepen U.S. Role in Iran War
stories.summary:
President Trump on Sunday endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection ahead of the Oct. 27 Knesset elections. In a lengthy Truth Social post addressed to the Israeli people, he called Netanyahu a "great warrior" and urged voters to back Likud. He praised Netanyahu as a critical ally in the war against Iran.

Trump also warned that Netanyahu's departure could leave the United States shouldering more of the conflict. The Iran war is now in its eighth month and has driven up oil and gasoline prices, a major issue for the administration ahead of U.S. midterm elections. Administration officials have faced questions on Sunday programs about whether earlier promises of lower gas prices have been kept.

The endorsement is a direct intervention in a foreign election during an active war involving U.S. forces. Supporters of the move see it as backing a close wartime partner, while critics are likely to question foreign interference and the risk of tying U.S. policy to one leader. The vote will determine the government guiding Israel's role in the war and the wider regional conflict, which has also drawn in Houthi forces and Gulf states.

stories.headline: Sanders Says Democrats Failed Working-Class Voters on Economics
stories.summary:
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said in an interview on MS NOW on Saturday that the Democratic Party failed working-class Americans on economic issues, contributing to their shift toward President Trump. Asked what Democrats had done wrong, he said the party has much to be proud of on civil rights, women's rights, gay rights and the environment, but "in terms of working-class issues, no, I don't think they've done a good job."

Sanders pointed to trade deals he said cost the country millions of manufacturing jobs and to years of unfulfilled promises. "They lost faith in the Democratic Party, and not unjustifiably," he said. The comments come as Democrats lead in midterm polling and fundraising with early voting underway.

The Republican National Committee, in a statement to Fox News Digital, said Democrats "can no longer claim to be the working class party" and accused them of appeasing their base. Fox's 2024 voter analysis found Trump won voters with household incomes of $50,000 to $99,999, while Harris carried those earning $100,000 or more. Democrats who share Sanders' critique argue the party should focus more on economic populism, while others say the party has delivered on economic policy and that Trump's record has hurt working families.

stories.headline: Update: Zelenskyy Says US Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine Has Resumed After Call With Trump Envoys
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday that the United States is sharing intelligence with Kyiv again after it was blocked for "some period of time." He made the remarks after a call with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Trump's envoys. Axios described it as the first call between Zelenskyy and senior U.S. officials since tensions spiked roughly 10 days ago, when Trump struck a diesel deal with Russia.

Zelenskyy said the discussions aimed at arranging new rounds of peace meetings as early as this week. He also said Ukraine's use of the SpaceX satellite system remains partially restricted, despite earlier signs it had been fully restored. According to Zelenskyy, the restrictions limit the military's ability to use drones to intercept Russian attack drones and to deliver supplies to soldiers on the front lines. In an NBC Meet the Press interview, he said he believes the American government directed SpaceX to slow Starshield internet speeds. Trump has denied restricting Ukraine's Starlink access.

The dispute has drawn criticism from some Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, and four GOP senators have joined a bipartisan call for a Pentagon probe of the disruption. Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on power infrastructure, with two people killed and at least 17 injured in the latest attacks. Whether the renewed intelligence flow and planned talks hold will be watched closely this week.

stories.headline: Update: Obama Condemns Probe of Ilhan Omar as Homan Says Investigators Have 'Strong Case'
stories.summary:
Former President Barack Obama issued a forceful denunciation of the Trump administration's legal pursuit of Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, in a lengthy post on X. The federal criminal investigation concerns suspicions that she fraudulently obtained U.S. citizenship decades ago, an allegation Omar has called "disgusting lies." Obama accused the administration of targeting its political opponents and of attempting to strip her of citizenship. Axios noted that Obama, who faced false claims from Trump for years that he was not an American citizen, is selective about when he weighs in.

On Saturday, White House border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that investigators have a "strong case" against Omar for possible immigration fraud. He said he had been informed by investigators that they have been following the matter closely. His comments came after federal agents searched Omar's Washington home last week.

Omar's attorneys have asked the Justice Department to return property agents seized during the search, calling the seizure "neither justified nor lawful" and asking that any recordings of the search be preserved. Administration supporters say the case is a routine fraud investigation that follows the evidence, while Democrats and critics describe it as political retaliation against a prominent critic of the president. No charges have been announced.

stories.headline: Vance Says US Has 'Decisively Won' Iran War 'In Some Ways' at CBS Town Hall
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance said Saturday that in "some ways" the United States has "decisively won" its war against Iran, while acknowledging that "the enemy gets a vote here, and they have responded in certain ways." He spoke at a CBS town hall. The remarks come as the conflict has widened, with Houthi strikes on Aden and a Saudi oil complex, record ship attacks near the Strait of Hormuz, and U.S. deliberations over options against Iran's underground nuclear sites.

Vance also defended Trump administration policies on gas prices, Iran's nuclear program and H-1B visas, and criticized Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan. He faced sharp questions from voters, some of whom said they had supported him and Trump. The exchange previewed the challenges he may face answering for the administration's record if he runs for president in 2028.

Supporters of the administration argue the military campaign has set back Iran's capabilities and that continued Iranian retaliation does not negate those gains. Critics, including Democrats, point to rising regional violence, energy-market disruption and the absence of a clear end to the war as evidence that claims of decisive victory are premature.

stories.headline: Trump Announces 15-Month Closure of East Potomac Golf Course Despite Court Challenge
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday that he will close the historic East Potomac Golf Course in Washington for 15 months starting Nov. 15 to redevelop it. He wrote that the project would make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World," open to the public and able to host events such as the U.S. Open, PGA Championship and Ryder Cup. He called the current course "old, broken, dilapidated."

The announcement came despite an ongoing legal fight. Last week a judge ordered a halt to redevelopment work until at least Oct. 26 after criticizing the government for starting large-scale tree removal over a holiday weekend with little notice to the court or plaintiffs. Trump's post did not acknowledge the litigation.

Democracy Forward, which represents the plaintiffs, said the 106-year-old course is part of a national park and recreation facility meant for everyone, and vowed to keep defending it. Opponents argue a high-end redesign would change the character of the space and make it less affordable. Trump's supporters view the project as part of his broader push to renovate Washington landmarks, many of which, including the White House ballroom, Kennedy Center changes and a planned arch, have also faced court challenges.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Waives Russia Sanctions Law Named for Late Sen. Lindsey Graham, Drawing Bipartisan Backlash
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump issued an executive order late Friday waiving many sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia that were due to take effect under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which he signed last month. The order told Congress the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details. The move follows other recent steps that critics say have drawn Washington closer to Moscow, including a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin.

Lawmakers from both parties condemned the decision over the weekend. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of giving Putin "the best birthday gift" and called it a "deal with the devil." Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) said she would prefer to keep sanctions pressure on Russia. A growing group of House Republicans is also warning they may block additional Pentagon funding unless the administration takes a tougher line on Russia. Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) defended the president, saying on Meet the Press that Trump is trying to facilitate negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the decision unfortunate and said it would encourage Russia to continue its attacks. He avoided directly criticizing Trump, said he still sees him as an ally, and said the American negotiating track will continue. He added that US intelligence sharing, which lapsed for about three days, has resumed, though Starlink access remains partially restricted. Congress is expected to take up a bipartisan effort to overturn the diesel deal when it returns after the election.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Launches More Than 1,000 Drones at Russia, Setting St. Petersburg Oil Terminal Ablaze
stories.summary:
Ukraine launched one of its largest aerial attacks of the war overnight Sunday, sending more than 1,000 drones toward Russia. The strikes set an oil export terminal in St. Petersburg ablaze and also hit a data center used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook. Russian state media called it one of the biggest drone attacks of the year.

At least one person was killed and five were wounded, and power was knocked out to thousands of residents. Russian officials said oil facilities were struck. Separately, Zelenskyy said Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight killed two people and that Moscow continues to violate the energy ceasefire.

The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Kyiv and Washington. President Trump has criticized Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, and last week he called one such move a disgrace. His decision to waive new Russia sanctions has added to the strain. Zelenskyy has said he is ready for fresh US-led talks and has renewed his appeal for Washington to pressure Moscow.

stories.headline: Deadly Attack at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport Kills a Dozen
stories.summary:
A dozen people were killed Saturday during what Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation described as a "brutal" attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Few details on the perpetrators or method were available in the initial reports.

The attack comes as the regional conflict widens. Separately, two people died when a Saudi reconnaissance helicopter crashed near the Yemen border, the first such fatalities the kingdom has reported since the latest flare-up with Houthi rebels. Clashes between Yemeni forces and Houthis have caused casualties on both sides, and aid agencies are warning of a humanitarian crisis.

Egypt's presidency says it will provide Saudi Arabia with support to defend its security and resources, though analysts say any Egyptian move will remain strictly defensive. France has also begun deploying forces to help defend Saudi oil facilities. The attack adds to concern about the widening Iran-related war and its effect on energy supplies.

stories.headline: Decades-Old GOP Winning Streaks Suddenly at Risk in Kansas, Texas and South Carolina
stories.summary:
Democrats are running surprisingly competitive midterm races in traditionally Republican territory, putting at risk GOP winning streaks that stretch back as far as the 1930s. Axios reports that Democrats hope ending political droughts in states such as Kansas, Texas and South Carolina will open inroads into long off-limits territory.

In Kansas, where Republicans have won Senate races since 1932, Sen. Roger Marshall faces a tougher-than-expected challenge from a Democrat. Elsewhere, Democratic Senate candidates have posted record fundraising numbers, and Democrats lead in polls and fundraising nationally.

Republicans remain hopeful. House Speaker Mike Johnson says he believes the GOP will hold its House majority despite Democratic momentum. Polls show 71 percent of US adults think the country is on the wrong track, and some GOP candidates are avoiding mention of Trump in their ads. Election Day is in about two weeks.

stories.headline: Wildfires Burn Homes in Southern California as Santa Ana Winds Drive Norte Fire
stories.summary:
A fast-moving wildfire fanned by strong Santa Ana winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday. The Norte Fire ignited at midday in San Clemente, and fire officials warned that wind gusts were causing a "dangerous rate of spread." About 6,000 homes were placed under evacuation orders, affecting roughly 16,000 residents in San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.

Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries. The Norte Fire is one of 13 fires burning across the state, and officials have not yet given a cause for it.

The fire is the latest test for California's emergency crews during a period of dangerous wind conditions. Evacuation orders remain in place, and officials are expected to provide updates on containment and damage assessments as winds persist.

stories.headline: Deadly Incident and Major Fire at Canadian Military Base in Alberta
stories.summary:
Canada's defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at CFB Wainwright in Alberta that caused a major fire. Defense Minister David McGuinty confirmed fatalities and injuries at one of the country's busiest military bases. Reports said large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals.

Officials have not given a cause or a death toll, citing the "very active and delicate" situation at the base. No details have been offered on how the fire began or whether it was accidental.

The incident comes as Canada is in a tense political moment, with Alberta having prepared for a vote on starting a legal process toward a separation referendum. Further information on casualties and the cause is expected as authorities investigate.

stories.headline: Update: Paris Riots Leave Widespread Damage as About 1,800 Arrested Across France
stories.summary:
France woke Sunday to scenes of widespread damage after a day of protests and riots. Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets, in marches that were largely peaceful. They were protesting rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Groups of masked rioters set fire to cars and buildings and looted shops in Paris, Marseille and Lille. In Marseille, protesters broke into city hall using a metal fence as a battering ram, and in Lille a McDonald's was set on fire and an Apple store looted. France's interior ministry said more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured, and the Retail and Trade Federation said about 1,500 shops were damaged.

Shopkeepers swept up glass outside luxury stores in Paris, where graffiti read "tax the rich." One shop owner said he did not believe the looters were genuine protesters and criticized the absence of police. The arrest total and scale of damage far exceed earlier figures, and the government's response is expected in coming days.

stories.headline: Car Driven Through Youth Soccer Game in Wichita, Kansas, Kills Child and Adult
stories.summary:
A vehicle drove through a soccer game at the Stryker Soccer Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday afternoon, killing a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man. Multiple other people were injured, police said.

The driver is in custody, and two juveniles were in the vehicle, according to Wichita police spokesman Aaron Moses, who spoke at a news conference. Police have not publicly detailed a motive or the circumstances that led to the vehicle entering the field.

Investigators are expected to release further information about the driver, the condition of the injured and any charges as the inquiry continues.
